title: The Tree That Changed the Water… and the Cross That Can Change You
paragraphs:
The Tree That Changed the Water… and the Cross That Can Change You
The Untold Miracle Behind the Bitter Water Made Sweet—and Why It May Be One of the Most Overlooked Pictures of Jesus Christ in the Entire Bible
You have probably tasted it before.
Not the water of Marah—but bitterness.
The kind that enters your life after betrayal.
After watching someone you love walk away.
After burying dreams you believed God Himself had planted.
And once it reaches the soul, nothing else feels sweet anymore.
Most people read the story of the bitter waters of Marah as if it were simply another miracle in Israel's wilderness journey. God made bad water drinkable. The people survived. The story moved on.
Every miracle whispers something much bigger.
The miracle at Marah was never just about water.
It was preparing the world for another tree.
One that would someday stand on a hill called Golgotha.
One that would not simply sweeten water...

The story begins in Exodus 15, immediately after one of Israel's greatest victories. God had just split the Red Sea. Pharaoh's army had drowned. Moses and Miriam led songs of worship. Celebration filled the camp.
The same people who had sung praises now questioned God.
That is one of the Bible's most painfully honest portraits of the human heart.
Sometimes our worship is only as deep as our comfort.
"When they came to Marah, they could not drink the waters of Marah, for they were bitter."
The root comes from מַר (mar) meaning "bitter."
The same word appears throughout Scripture describing deep personal suffering.
After losing her husband and sons she said:
"Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara."
It described the condition of the human soul.
Isn't that where many people are today?
Yet carrying invisible Marah everywhere they go.
But the water they desperately needed could not satisfy them.
Sometimes God allows us to discover that what we thought would heal us cannot actually heal us.
only to discover the water is bitter.
Then Exodus 15:25 records one of the strangest miracles in all of Scripture.
"And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD showed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet..."
God did not remove the water.
Throughout the Old Testament this word quietly points toward something much greater.
The Septuagint—the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament—uses:
The exact same Greek word appears repeatedly in the New Testament when describing the Cross.
"The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging Him on a tree."
The Holy Spirit intentionally preserves this connection.
The tree at Marah was never random.
The bitterness did not corrupt the tree.
That is exactly what Jesus did.
Our sin did not make Him sinful.
Our curse did not overpower Him.
His holiness transformed what sin had poisoned.
The Cross is God's eternal answer to Marah.
Everything poisonous in humanity met the Tree.
And instead of the Tree becoming bitter...
Moses did not invent the solution.
Human wisdom could never have discovered it.
The Cross was never humanity's idea.
It was God's eternal plan before the foundation of the world.
Even more astonishing is what comes immediately after the miracle.
"I am the LORD who heals you."
Not merely the healer of bodies.
The healer of what no therapist, achievement, relationship, or amount of money can completely restore.
God often brings His people to bitter places before revealing Himself more deeply.
Not because He delights in suffering.
But because healing often begins where self-sufficiency finally ends.
Jesus echoed this truth centuries later.
"If anyone thirsts, let him come to Me and drink."
Because He Himself would become that Tree.
Even the Apostle Peter connects these truths.
"He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree..."
Every appearance of the tree points forward.
This also explains why the miracle seems strangely simple.
Throwing a piece of wood into bitter water should accomplish nothing.
Unless God has declared that the wood represents His coming salvation.
Marah is not primarily about chemistry.
Perhaps today your own water feels bitter.
Maybe years of disappointment have convinced you that bitterness will always define your story.
But the Gospel tells another story.
Jesus does not merely ask you to ignore your bitterness.

He does not promise that every painful circumstance instantly disappears. Scripture never teaches that. Rather, through union with Christ, suffering is no longer meaningless, and bitterness no longer has the final word (Romans 8:28; 2 Corinthians 4:16–18). The Cross changes the deepest reality of our lives by reconciling us to God and beginning the lifelong work of making us new.
That is the pattern of Scripture.
It can become scandal to grace too.
Perhaps that is why this miracle sits quietly between the Red Sea and Mount Sinai.
The Law had not yet been given.
That has always been the order of redemption.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that we are saved "by grace... through faith... not a result of works." Good works are the fruit of salvation, not the cause of it (Ephesians 2:10).
You never know whether this could be the moment God uses His Word to point them to the true Tree that heals.
Return to it whenever bitterness whispers that God has abandoned you. The same Lord who revealed the tree to Moses has revealed His Son to the world.
In that way, your generosity becomes one practical way of participating in the spread of the Good News and glorifying God through the stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
The sweetest water you will ever taste is not found where life is easiest—but where Christ meets you in your deepest need.
